photosensitivity.title: Photosensitivity warning
photosensitivity.body: This protocol shows flashing, high-contrast or moving images. If you or the person being recorded have photosensitive epilepsy, or have ever had a seizure with flashing lights, do not continue.
photosensitivity.stop: You can stop at any time with Stop or the Esc key. Stop at once if you feel dizzy, notice twitching or changes in your vision, or feel unwell in any way.

runner.disclaimer: This is not a medical assessment or diagnosis. You can stop at any time.
runner.stopBody: What you have done so far is kept. You cannot resume this run.

help.title: Where the sensors sit
help.intro: The band holds four dry electrodes against the skin: two on the forehead just above the eyebrows, two behind the ears. The lights follow the band from left to right as you wear it, so the leftmost light is the sensor behind your left ear.

form.nothing_to_set: Nothing to set: this block works as it is.

inspector.title: Block
inspector.label: Name
inspector.kind_hint: The type is chosen when the block is added and cannot be changed here.
inspector.condition_hint: A word for what this block is in your experiment (calm, scary, control). Blocks with the same condition are compared together in the review and in the exported data. Leave empty if you are not comparing anything.
inspector.skippable: The participant may skip this block
inspector.unknown_kind_hint: This app does not know this block type. Its settings are kept untouched.
inspector.around: Timing around the block, and analysis
inspector.pre_fixation_s_hint: Shows a fixation cross for this long before the block starts, to settle the eyes.
inspector.jitter_s_hint: Adds a random time, up to this much, to the cross before the block, so the participant cannot predict the exact start.
inspector.post_rest_s_hint: An empty screen for this long after the block, to let the signal come back to rest.
inspector.skippable_hint: Shows a Skip button. The skip is written in the timeline, so you know the block was not completed.
inspector.video_hint: The video the person watches during the block, looped and muted.

monitor.empty: Drag a video or an element onto the timeline below. What the participant will see shows up here.
monitor.split_hint: Pause the video where you want the cut, then split: you get two clips over the same video, and can put a questionnaire or a rest between them.

soundtrack.title: Sound
soundtrack.empty: Drag a sound here to play it over the blocks — background music, a spoken instruction.
soundtrack.only_audio: Only sounds go on this lane.
soundtrack.drag_stop: Drag to the block it should stop at
soundtrack.label: Name
soundtrack.loop_needs_stop: A looping sound needs somewhere to stop: the end of the protocol or of a block.
soundtrack.note: Sounds play over the blocks instead of taking a turn. For a sound that must be time-locked to the EEG, use an audio block instead.

audio.label: Sound
audio.hint: Plays a sound on a dark screen.

text.label: Reading
text.hint: A text the participant reads at their own pace.

image-sequence.label: Image sequence
image-sequence.hint: Images shown one after another, each with its own marker.

go-no-go.label: Signal Navigator
go-no-go.hint: The go/no-go game: dock the cargo, let the debris pass.

breathing.label: Paced breathing
breathing.hint: A circle that grows and shrinks to breathe with.

quiz.label: Quiz
quiz.hint: Questions with right and wrong answers.

flanker.label: Arrows (flanker)
flanker.hint: Which way does the middle arrow point? The arrows around it may disagree. With cues it is the Attention Network Test.

n-back.label: Letter memory (n-back)
n-back.hint: Letters one at a time: press when this one is the letter from a few steps ago.

coding.label: Symbol coding
coding.hint: Match symbols to digits against the clock: how many in ninety seconds.

heartbeat.label: Heartbeat counting
heartbeat.hint: Count your own heartbeats between two tones, without touching your pulse.

baseline.label: Resting baseline
baseline.hint: Sitting still, eyes open or closed: what every other block is compared to.

rest.label: Rest
rest.hint: A break between blocks, timed or until the participant continues.

fixation.label: Fixation cross
fixation.hint: A cross to look at, to settle the eyes before a stimulus.

questionnaire.label: Questionnaire
questionnaire.hint: Asks how the participant feels (SAM) or your own questions.

instructions.label: Instructions
instructions.hint: Text on screen that explains what comes next.

prompt.label: Prompt
prompt.hint: A short line on screen, then on with the run.

neurofeedback.label: Neurofeedback
neurofeedback.hint: A video that brightens while the chosen brain rhythm is in its target zone.

text.line: Tell the participant what happens next.

go-no-go-cued.label: Signal Navigator, with beacon
go-no-go-cued.hint: A green or red beacon comes first and changes the rule.

flanker-ant.label: Attention networks
flanker-ant.hint: The arrows task with warning and location cues: alerting, orienting, conflict.

n-back-self-paced.label: Self-paced n-back
n-back-self-paced.hint: The same letters, but each one stays until the participant presses Continue.

neurofeedback.label: Neurofeedback
neurofeedback.hint: Pick its video in the settings. A baseline comes first and sets the threshold.

markers.label: Event names
markers.help: The name this moment gets in the recording's event timeline. Change it only if your analysis expects a specific name.

lines/text.label: Text
lines/text.help: What the participant reads. A new line in the box is a new line on screen.

lines/holdMs.label: Stays on screen (ms)
lines/holdMs.help: How long this line is shown before the next one. 1000 ms is one second.

lines/marker.label: Event name
lines/marker.help: The name this moment gets in the recording's event timeline. Change it only if your analysis expects a specific name.

lines.label: Lines of text
lines.help: Shown one after another, in this order.

advance/mode.label: The block ends
advance/mode.help: After a fixed time, when the participant presses the button, or whichever comes first.

advance/label.label: Button text
advance/label.help: What the button that moves on says, for example Continue or Start.

advance/ms.label: Duration (ms)
advance/ms.help: How long the block lasts when it ends on its own.

advance/minMs.label: Button appears after (ms)
advance/minMs.help: The button is disabled until then, so nobody skips the text without reading it.

advance/maxMs.label: Moves on by itself after (ms)
advance/maxMs.help: A time limit for a participant who never presses the button.

footnote.label: Small print
footnote.help: A quiet line under the text, for a reminder like 'you can stop at any time'.

markers/*.help: The name this moment gets in the recording's event timeline. Change it only if your analysis expects a specific name.

allowPause.label: The participant can pause
allowPause.help: Off keeps every participant on the same timeline, which is what you want when comparing them.

endOn.label: The block ends
endOn.help: When the video finishes, or after a fixed time even if the video is longer.

durationMs.label: Fixed time (ms)
durationMs.help: Only used when the block ends after a fixed time.

start_s.label: Start at (s)
start_s.help: Play from this second of the video instead of its beginning. Splitting a clip on the timeline fills this in.

end_s.label: Stop at (s)
end_s.help: Stop at this second of the video instead of its end.

cues.label: Moments to mark
cues.help: Points in the video you want to find again in the recording: a jump scare, a scene change. Each becomes an event on the timeline.

cues/atS.label: At (s)
cues/atS.help: Seconds from the start of the video.

cues/label.label: Name
cues/label.help: How the event is called in the timeline.

cues/note.label: Note
cues/note.help: For you; the participant never sees it.

start_s.label: Start at (s)
start_s.help: Skip the beginning of the file: play from this second.

end_s.label: Stop at (s)
end_s.help: Cut the end of the file: stop at this second.

min_s.label: Shortest reading time (s)
min_s.help: Continue is disabled until then, so the text is actually read.

eyes.label: Eyes
eyes.help: Eyes closed gives the strongest alpha rhythm and is the reference the review page compares every block to. Eyes open is closer to how the other blocks are done.

duration_s.label: Duration (s)
duration_s.help: One to two minutes is usual. Under 30 s is too short to be a stable reference.

end_tone.label: Play a tone at the end
end_tone.help: So a participant with closed eyes knows when to open them.

mode.label: The break ends
mode.help: After a fixed time, or when the participant feels ready.

duration_s.label: Duration (s)
duration_s.help: Used when the break ends after a fixed time.

message.label: Message
message.help: What the screen says during the break.

duration_s.label: Duration (s)
duration_s.help: How long the cross stays. One second or two before a stimulus is usual.

n.label: Trials
n.help: How many rows of arrows. 96 takes about three minutes; with cues use a multiple of 8 so every combination comes up equally often.

congruentRatio.label: Share of agreeing rows
congruentRatio.help: The fraction of rows whose outer arrows point the same way as the middle one, from 0 to 1. At 0.5 the disagreement cannot be predicted.

cues.label: Cues before the row
cues.help: Leave empty for the plain arrows task. With cues the row appears above or below the cross and a brief asterisk may come first: this is the Attention Network Test. Use all four for its three scores.

practice.label: This is a practice round
practice.help: Marks every trial as practice: played, never scored.

feedback.label: Say right or wrong
feedback.help: Shows Correct, Wrong side or Too slow after each row. Use it for practice; in the real block it changes how people respond.

maxRun.label: Longest streak
maxRun.help: The most rows of the same type in a row.

cueMs.label: Cue stays on (ms)
cueMs.help: 100 ms is the standard: long enough to see, too short to look at.

cueTargetMs.label: Cue to row (ms)
cueTargetMs.help: The quiet gap between the cue going off and the row appearing.

stimulusMs.label: Time to answer (ms)
stimulusMs.help: The row stays up until an answer or this long, then counts as too slow.

itiMs.label: Pause between rows (ms)
itiMs.help: Shortest and longest time on the cross between two rows. Varying it stops people answering to the rhythm.

pace.label: Pace
pace.help: Fixed: every letter gets the same time, answered or not - the standard n-back. Self-paced: each letter stays until the participant presses Continue, with Match before it; it takes away the time pressure and records how long each letter was kept.

n.label: Letters
n.help: How many letters are shown. 60 takes two and a half minutes.

load.label: How far back
load.help: 1: is it the same as the previous letter? 2: the same as the one before that? 3 is hard for most people. Compare blocks of different loads to see effort rise.

matchRatio.label: Share of matches
matchRatio.help: The fraction of letters that repeat the one from that far back, from 0 to 1. About 0.3 is standard.

lureRatio.label: Share of near misses
lureRatio.help: Letters that repeat one step off: they feel like a match and must be let go. They tell remembering the order from merely recognising a recent letter. 0 turns them off.

practice.label: This is a practice round
practice.help: Marks every trial as practice: played, never scored.

stimulusMs.label: Letter stays on (ms)
stimulusMs.help: The letter disappears after this long; the answer can still come.

isiMs.label: Blank after the letter (ms)
isiMs.help: The pace is fixed: every letter gets its time plus this blank, answered or not.

gapMs.label: Blank after Continue (ms)
gapMs.help: A short blank between letters, so two equal letters in a row read as two.

duration_s.label: Length (seconds)
duration_s.help: How long the participant keeps matching. 90 seconds is the standard; the score is how many they get right in that time.

practice.label: This is a practice round
practice.help: Marks every answer as practice: played, never scored.

pairs.label: Symbols in the key
pairs.help: How many symbol-digit pairs to look up, from 2 to 9. Nine is the standard; fewer makes it easier to memorise and less of a speed test.

itiMs.label: Pause between symbols (ms)
itiMs.help: A brief blank after each answer, so two identical-looking moments are not mistaken for one.

intervals_s.label: Counting rounds (seconds each)
intervals_s.help: One number per round. Use different lengths, or people multiply a guessed heart rate by the time. The headband's pulse sensor counts the real beats.

shuffle.label: Rounds in a random order
shuffle.help: A different order each session, so the lengths cannot be learned.

confidence.label: Ask how sure they are
confidence.help: After each round. How well confidence follows accuracy is its own measure, and the more telling one in anxiety.

ready_s.label: Get-ready time (seconds)
ready_s.help: How long the instruction is shown before the starting tone.

inhaleMs.label: Breathe in (ms)
inhaleMs.help: How long the circle grows. 4500 ms with the same out is about 6.5 breaths a minute.

holdMs.label: Hold (ms)
holdMs.help: A pause between in and out. Leave empty for none.

lines.label: Text after the breaths
lines.help: Optional lines shown one after another once the last breath ends, in place of the circle. To tell the participant what comes next, an Instructions block after this one is clearer.

variant.label: Version
variant.help: Simple: dock the blue cargo, let the orange debris pass. With a beacon: a green or red light comes first and changes the rule, which is harder.

n.label: Objects
n.help: How many objects cross the screen. 100 takes about two minutes.

goRatio.label: Share of cargo
goRatio.help: The fraction of objects to dock, from 0 to 1. Around 0.7 makes docking a habit, which is what makes holding back hard.

validGoRatio.label: Share of green beacon + cargo
validGoRatio.help: The fraction of trials where the participant should dock, from 0 to 1.

practice.label: Practice round first
practice.help: A few unscored objects before the real ones.

travelMs.label: Crossing time (ms)
travelMs.help: How long an object takes to cross the screen: a shortest and a longest time, picked at random between the two. Shorter is harder.

itiMs.label: Pause between objects (ms)
itiMs.help: Shortest and longest empty time between two objects.

cueMs.label: Beacon stays on (ms)
cueMs.help: Shortest and longest time the beacon is lit.

cueTargetMs.label: Beacon to object (ms)
cueTargetMs.help: Shortest and longest wait between the beacon and the object.

maxRun.label: Most cargo in a row
maxRun.help: Keeps the random order from producing long streaks that make the task predictable.

maxNogoRun.label: Most debris in a row
maxNogoRun.help: Same, for the objects to let pass.

maxCueRun.label: Most same beacons in a row
maxCueRun.help: Limits streaks of the same beacon colour.

maxOutcomeRun.label: Most same answers in a row
maxOutcomeRun.help: Limits streaks of trials with the same right answer.

nogoMix.label: Kinds of 'hold' trials
nogoMix.help: How the trials where the participant must not dock are split. The three shares add up to 1.

items.label: Images
items.help: Shown in this order, or shuffled.

items/id.label: Name
items/id.help: How this image is called in the timeline.

items/class.label: Category
items/class.help: A group the image belongs to (faces, houses), for comparing categories later.

jitterMs.label: Random extra gap (ms)
jitterMs.help: Up to this much is added to each gap, so the rhythm is not predictable.

shuffle.label: Shuffle the order
shuffle.help: A different order per participant, the same for the same participant and seed.

instrument.label: Questionnaire
instrument.help: SAM asks how pleasant and how activated the participant feels, with pictures. VAS is a single slider. NASA-TLX measures workload. Custom uses your own questions below.

prompt.label: Question on top
prompt.help: Shown above the scales, for example 'How did the video make you feel?'

items.label: Your questions
items.help: Only used by the Custom questionnaire.

items/id.label: Short name
items/id.help: How the answer is called in the exported data.

scenes/correct.label: Right answer (number)
scenes/correct.help: The position of the right answer in the list, starting from 0.

feedback.label: Say if the answer was right
feedback.help: Off keeps the participant from learning during the quiz.

signal.label: Brain rhythm
signal.help: What the feedback follows, measured in the browser from the headband. A band is its share of all the power between 1 and 45 Hz; a ratio divides one band by the other.

direction.label: Reward when the value is
direction.help: Above or below the threshold. Left empty, theta, beta and theta/beta are trained down and the others up.

channels.label: Electrodes
channels.help: Left empty, theta and theta/beta are read on the forehead (AF7, AF8) and the others behind the ears (TP9, TP10): at the forehead, beta and SMR are mostly the muscle above the eyebrows.

effect.label: The picture
effect.help: Brightness only, or brightness plus a blur that clears in target.

duration_s.label: Training time (seconds)
duration_s.help: How long the feedback runs after the baseline. Up to 30 minutes; long blocks tire people.

baseline_s.label: Baseline (seconds)
baseline_s.help: The video at a steady brightness while the signal is measured; it sets the threshold. 0 for none, which needs a fixed threshold.

threshold/mode.label: Threshold from
threshold/mode.help: From this person's baseline today, or a fixed number that stays the same across sessions.

threshold/target_fraction.label: Share of the baseline in target
threshold/target_fraction.help: 0.4 sets the threshold so that 40% of the baseline would have been rewarded.

threshold/value.label: Fixed threshold
threshold/value.help: A share between 0 and 1 for a band (0.25 is a quarter of the power), or the ratio itself.

window_s.label: Analysis window (seconds)
window_s.help: Each value is computed over this much signal. Longer is steadier and slower.

smoothing_s.label: Smoothing (seconds)
smoothing_s.help: How much the value is averaged over time before it is compared with the threshold.

ramp_s.label: Picture response (seconds)
ramp_s.help: How long a full swing from dim to bright takes. The brightness never changes fast enough to flash, whatever this says.

min_level.label: Brightness out of target
min_level.help: How dim the picture gets: 0.4 is 40% of full brightness.

artefact/max_ptp_uv.label: Largest swing (µV)
artefact/max_ptp_uv.help: A window with a bigger swing (a blink, a movement) holds the picture instead of moving it.

artefact/max_muscle.label: Muscle share limit
artefact/max_muscle.help: A window with more than this share of power above 30 Hz (jaw, frowning) holds the picture.

beta.promptText: Brain Trails is in a closed beta. Beta testers get new protocols and features first, for free, and we ask them what they think. Applying takes a few questions.
beta.promptLaterHint: You can apply any time from your account.

beta.notOnList: You are not on the list.
beta.wantsBeta: I would like to be a beta tester.
beta.intendedUse: How you expect to use it
beta.intendedUseQuestion: How do you expect to use it?

compare.trailAria: The trail of {block}, on the session's terrain

frame.taskAria: The task as it looked at this moment of {block}
frame.noTrials: No trials recorded in this block

baseline.open: Eyes open, looking at the screen

frame.nothing: Nothing recorded to show for this kind of block

compare.byTime: Coloured from the start of the block to its end.
compare.averagePerson: Average person: {value} ({n, plural, one {# person} other {# people}})
compare.averagePending: Average person: shown from {min} people, {n} so far
compare.noAverage: No one else has done this block yet
compare.noBlocks: This recording has no protocol blocks to compare. The trail of the whole session is below.
compare.disclaimer: Exploratory, not diagnostic. These describe one recording, not a person.

missing.not_ready: Not computed for this recording yet

alpha.name: Alpha
alpha.meaning: Share of the signal's power in the 8–12 Hz band. It rises when you relax with eyes closed and drops when you look and pay attention.

beta.name: Beta
beta.meaning: Share of power in the 13–30 Hz band. It tends to rise with alert, focused or tense activity.

theta.name: Theta
theta.meaning: Share of power in the 4–8 Hz band. It rises with drowsiness, and at the front of the head with effortful focus and memory.

delta.name: Delta
delta.meaning: Share of power below 4 Hz. Awake, much of it comes from movement and blinks, so a high value often means a noisier stretch.

entropy.name: Entropy
entropy.meaning: How hard it is to guess the next brain state from the current one, in bits. Low: the signal follows a routine; high: it wanders unpredictably.

recurrence.name: Recurrence
recurrence.meaning: How often a move goes back to a state already visited in this stretch. High: the signal circles familiar places; low: it keeps finding new ones.

modularity.name: Modularity
modularity.meaning: How much windows of the same kind of trial gather in the same states. Near 0: kinds of trial mix freely; higher: each has places of its own.

diameter.name: Diameter
diameter.meaning: How wide the range of brain states covered is, in ball widths of the map. Larger: the signal ranged further.

stretching.name: Stretching
stretching.meaning: The average step from one moment to the next, as a share of the diameter. High: big jumps across the space; low: small, gradual drift.

accuracy.name: Right actions
accuracy.meaning: Share of trials where the person did what the task asked. Read it with false alarms: pressing less can raise it on its own.

reaction_time.name: Reaction time
reaction_time.meaning: Typical time from the target appearing to the press (the median). Lower is faster.

rt_spread.name: Reaction spread
rt_spread.meaning: How much the reaction time varied from trial to trial. Lower is steadier.

hit_rate.name: Targets caught
hit_rate.meaning: Share of targets that got an answer. Missed targets pull it down.

false_alarms.name: False alarms
false_alarms.meaning: Share of non-targets pressed anyway: acting before checking. Lower is more careful.

privacy.title: What happens to your data.
privacy.draft: Brain Trails is a non-clinical research prototype, and this note is a draft published pending legal review. It describes what the system actually does today. It will be replaced by a reviewed policy, and we will tell you when that happens.
privacy.intro: Protecting the privacy of the people who use Brain Trails matters to us more than anything else we do with this prototype — we are asking you for recordings of your brain, and we do not take that lightly. We are making every effort to keep your data secure and to bring this note fully in line with the law that applies to it. We have tried hard to describe only what is true today rather than what we intend to build, and where something is not built yet, this note says so.

whatItIs.title: 1. What Brain Trails is, and is not
whatItIs.p1: Brain Trails is provided for informational and wellness purposes. Unless Lumentis Analytics Inc. says otherwise in writing, it is not a medical device and is not intended to diagnose, treat, cure, prevent or monitor any disease or medical condition. It does not provide medical advice.
whatItIs.p2: Do not make medical decisions based on it. Talk to a qualified health-care professional about symptoms, diagnosis or treatment.

whoWeAre.title: 2. Who we are
whoWeAre.p1: Lumentis Analytics Inc. is responsible for the personal information processed through Brain Trails.
whoWeAre.addressee: Lumentis Analytics Inc., Attn: Privacy Officer
whoWeAre.postalAddress: 329 Howe Street, Unit 272, Vancouver, British Columbia V6C 3N2, Canada

collect.title: 3. What we collect
collect.p1: Your account. Your email address, your password (stored only as a hash, never as text we can read), and an account identifier we generate.
collect.p2: What you tell us about yourself. Your name, year of birth and handedness, and — if you choose to give them — details such as sex at birth, sleep, caffeine, medications, and neurological or psychiatric conditions. Several of these are health-related and sensitive. Only the few that make a recording interpretable are required, none of them at sign-up, and the rest are offered and never demanded.
collect.p3: Your recordings. The EEG captured during a session, signal-quality and device information, your responses and timings during an exercise, and everything derived from them: features, metrics, projections, visualisations and reports.
collect.p4: EEG recordings and what we derive from them may be sensitive personal information. Depending on the context they may be treated as health-related or biometric information.
collect.p5: Technical information. Ordinary server logs, browser and device type, IP address, and the session cookie that keeps you signed in.

use.title: 4. What we do with it
use.p1: We use it to run the service: to keep your account, to receive and process your recordings, to compute the analyses and reports you asked for, to show you your history, to keep the service secure and working, and to answer you when you write to us.
use.p2: Improving Brain Trails itself. We use recordings and derived data to check and improve the accuracy and reliability of what Brain Trails does — whether a reading is sound, whether a metric behaves, why something failed. This is part of running the service you are using.
use.p3: Broader research — only if you say yes. Separately, and only with the optional consent you can give at sign-up and change at any time on your account page, we may keep and use your pseudonymised recordings and derived data for scientific research going beyond running and improving this service. Saying no changes nothing about your account, your recordings or your results. If you withdraw, we stop using your data for research from that point; we cannot undo research already done, or recover data that has been irreversibly anonymised.
use.p4: We do not sell your personal information, your recordings or anything derived from them, and we do not use them for advertising or behavioural tracking of any kind.

consent.title: 5. Consent
consent.p1: We ask for two things separately. The first is consent to process your recordings and account data in order to provide Brain Trails at all — without it there is no service to give you. The second is the optional research consent above.
consent.p2: You can withdraw the optional one at any time from your account page. You can withdraw the first by deleting your account, also from your account page, or by writing to us. Withdrawing does not undo processing already carried out.

pseudonymised.title: 6. Pseudonymised is not anonymous
pseudonymised.p1: Your recordings and everything derived from them are stored against a randomly generated identifier rather than your name or your email, and the files themselves carry no identifying detail in their names or their contents. Your identity lives in a separate database.
pseudonymised.p2: That is a real protection, and it is not anonymity. While we can reconnect an identifier to you — and through our own account system, we can — the data is still personal information, and this note treats it as such throughout. We will not describe anything as anonymous unless it has been processed so that a person is no longer reasonably identifiable from it.

storage.title: 7. Where it is stored
storage.p1: Lumentis Analytics Inc. is a Canadian company. Recordings, files and the application database are stored in Frankfurt, Germany. The application itself is served by Vercel, whose network is global, so requests may be handled outside that region even though the data at rest is not.
storage.p2: Authorised Lumentis personnel may access the data from Canada and Italy, where necessary to run, maintain and support the service.

security.title: 8. Security
security.p1: Some of what protects your data comes from the platforms we build on, by default and without us configuring anything:

platforms.1: Files are encrypted at rest. Amazon S3 applies AES-256 server-side encryption to every new object as a baseline that cannot be switched off (<link>AWS documents this</link>).
platforms.2: The database is encrypted at rest and reached over TLS; see <link>Neon’s security overview</link>.
platforms.3: Traffic between your browser and us travels over HTTPS.

security.p2: And some of it is our own doing:

own.1: Passwords are stored only as Argon2 hashes. We cannot read them.
own.2: Your files are never public. They are reached through links that are generated for one file and expire within minutes.
own.3: Access to the systems holding recordings is limited to the small number of people who run the service.
own.4: Identity is kept in a different place from the recordings, as described in section 6.

security.p3: Linking to those pages tells you what our providers do; it is not a claim that everything on our side is configured perfectly. No system is completely secure, and we cannot promise that yours will never be breached. What we can promise is that we will investigate anything we suspect and tell you where the law requires it — and, for something this sensitive, where it does not but you would obviously want to know.

retention.title: 9. Keeping it, and deleting it
retention.p1: We keep your account and your recordings while your account exists and this prototype is running. We have not set a fixed retention period yet and we are not going to invent one here: you can export or delete everything yourself, at any time, from your account page.
retention.p2: Because this is a prototype, data may also be removed when we reset an environment. We will give you notice before doing that deliberately.
retention.p3: When you delete your account, we delete your personal information: your recordings and the files behind them, the analyses and reports derived from them, your profile — including any health-related answers you gave — and the account itself.
retention.p4: One narrow exception. We keep a minimal record that consent was given and later withdrawn or deleted, so that we can show we asked properly and honoured your request. That record contains no EEG data, no health information, no name and no email address — only an account identifier, which version of this note was agreed to, and when. Once your account is deleted, that identifier no longer points to anything we hold.
retention.p5: Backups are not edited by hand. Copies of data held in backups disappear as those backups expire on their normal cycle.

disclosure.title: 10. Who else sees it
disclosure.p1: We do not sell your personal information and we do not share it for advertising. It is disclosed only to the providers who host and run the service on our behalf under contract — today our cloud storage, database, hosting and email providers — to professional advisers where genuinely necessary, where the law or a valid legal process requires it, to protect people from harm, in connection with a business transaction subject to privacy law, and to anyone you ask us to share it with.

rights.title: 11. Your rights
rights.p1: Two of these you can exercise yourself, right now, from your account page: export everything we hold about you, and delete your account. You can also grant or withdraw the optional research consent there.
rights.p2: For anything else — access, correction, restricting or objecting to particular processing, or asking what we have disclosed — write to <email>{privacyEmail}</email>. A person reads that address. We may need to confirm who you are before we act.
rights.p3: If you are not satisfied with how we have handled something, you can complain to the Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada, or to the Office of the Information and Privacy Commissioner for British Columbia.

cookies.title: 12. Cookies
cookies.p1: We use one cookie, to keep you signed in, and browser storage for small preferences such as whether you chose the light or the dark theme. No advertising cookies, no third-party analytics, no tracking pixels. If you block the session cookie you will not be able to sign in.
cookies.p2: A session cookie or a stored identifier does not make your recordings anonymous. If an identifier lets us find your data, that data is still personal information.

age.title: 13. Age
age.p1: Brain Trails is for people aged 18 and over. We do not knowingly open accounts for anyone younger. If you believe someone under 18 has created an account, write to us and we will delete it.

otherServices.title: 14. Other services
otherServices.p1: Brain Trails works with a Muse EEG headband, which is made and supported by another company under its own privacy policy. The same goes for the infrastructure providers named above. We encourage you to read their notices.

changes.title: 15. Changes to this note
changes.p1: When we change this note in a way that matters, we will publish a new version and ask you to read and agree to it the next time you sign in. The version is at the top of this page and is recorded against your account when you agree, so there is always a record of what you actually agreed to.

contact.title: 16. Contact
contact.p1: Questions, requests or complaints: <email>{privacyEmail}</email>, or Lumentis Analytics Inc., Attn: Privacy Officer, 329 Howe Street, Unit 272, Vancouver, British Columbia V6C 3N2, Canada.

attention-networks.title: Attention Networks
attention-networks.summary: The arrows game with warning flashes: alerting, orienting and conflict, separately.
attention-networks.description: The Attention Network Test. A flash may warn you that the arrows are coming, or show you where; the arrows may agree or not. Comparing those cases gives three scores: how much a warning helps, how much knowing the place helps, and what conflict costs. Two rounds of four minutes.
attention-networks.contentWarning: Arrows and brief flashes appear on the screen for about eight minutes, and you answer quickly. You can stop at any time.

0.text: First you rest, then two rounds of a game with arrows.

Keep your eyes on the cross.
A row of arrows will appear above or below it.

1.text:
Which way does the MIDDLE arrow point?
Press the left or right arrow key, or tap the side.

2.text:
Sometimes a star flashes first. It tells you the arrows are coming,
and sometimes where. Keep looking at the cross.

3.text: A short practice first. It will tell you how you did.

0.text:
That was practice.
Now two rounds of four minutes, with a break between.

config.message: Rest your eyes. Round two starts by itself.

0.text: All done.

config.footnote: This is not a medical test or diagnosis.

breath-pacing.title: Breath Pacing
breath-pacing.summary: Five minutes of slow breathing, six breaths a minute, between two rests.
breath-pacing.description: Breathe in for four seconds and out for six, following a circle. Rest before and after with your eyes closed, and say how you feel each time, so the change has two ends. With a headband that has a pulse sensor your heart rate is measured along.

0.text: First you rest, then you breathe with a circle for five minutes.

config.prompt: Think of how you feel right now.

0.text:
Breathe in as the circle grows,
out as it shrinks.

1.text:
Out is longer than in. Let it be easy:
if you feel light-headed, breathe normally.

config.prompt: Think of how you feel now.

0.text: All done.

config.footnote: This is not a medical test or diagnosis.

emotion-video.title: Emotion video
emotion-video.summary: Short film clips in random order, each followed by how it made you feel.
emotion-video.description: A resting baseline, then cleared film clips in an order drawn for this session, each followed by a rest and a Self-Assessment Manikin, then a closing baseline.
emotion-video.contentWarning: This protocol shows short film clips chosen to evoke emotions, some of them unpleasant. You can stop at any time.

config.prompt: Think of how you felt while watching the clip.

flanker-control.title: Flanker Control
flanker-control.summary: Which way does the middle arrow point, when the ones around it disagree?
flanker-control.description: A row of five arrows, answered as fast as you can. When the outer arrows point the other way you slow down and slip more often: that cost is how hard your attention works to shut out what is next to the target, and your brain's response to a slip is measured too.
flanker-control.contentWarning: Arrows flash on the screen for about four minutes, and you answer quickly. You can stop at any time.

0.text: First you rest, then a quick game with arrows.
A row of arrows will appear.

1.text:
Which way does the MIDDLE arrow point?
Press the left or right arrow key, or tap the side.

2.text:
The other arrows may point the other way. Ignore them.
Be fast, but be right.

3.text: A short practice first. It will tell you how you did.

0.text:
That was practice.
Now about four minutes, without the hints.
All done.

config.footnote: This is not a medical test or diagnosis.

free-recording.title: Free recording
free-recording.summary: Record your EEG with nothing on screen, for as long as you like.
free-recording.description: No stimulus: the headband records while you rest, read or meditate, and you stop when you are done. The simplest way to see your own trail.

interoceptive-focus.title: Interoceptive Focus
interoceptive-focus.summary: Count your own heartbeats between two tones, without touching your pulse.
interoceptive-focus.description: Four rounds of silent counting, then how many and how sure. The headband's pulse sensor counts the real beats, so you see how closely you feel your own heart - and whether your confidence follows your accuracy, which is the more telling part.

0.text: First you rest, then you listen for your own heartbeat, four times.

1.text: About seven minutes in all. Sit comfortably, hands resting, sound on.

config.prompt: Think of how you feel right now.

0.text: Between two tones, silently count your heartbeats.

1.text:
Do not touch your wrist or neck. Just feel.
Count only the beats you really feel. Do not guess.

2.text: Then type how many. Feeling few or none is a normal answer.

0.text: All done.

config.footnote: This is not a medical test or diagnosis.

processing-speed.title: Processing Speed
processing-speed.summary: Match symbols to numbers against the clock, twice for ninety seconds.
processing-speed.description: A table pairs nine symbols with nine digits; a symbol appears and you press its digit, as many as you can. One of the most sensitive short measures of mental speed there is: it moves with sleep, age and fatigue. The table changes each round.

0.text: A short rest, then two rounds of matching symbols to numbers against the clock.
A table at the top pairs each symbol with a number.

1.text:
A symbol appears in the middle.
Press its number, on the keyboard or on the screen.

2.text: As many as you can, without mistakes. A short practice first.

0.text:
Now ninety seconds. The table has changed.
Go as fast as you can while staying right.

config.message: Shake out your hands. One more round, with a new table.

0.text: All done.

config.footnote: This is not a medical test or diagnosis.

resting-baseline.title: Resting baseline
resting-baseline.summary: One minute eyes open, one minute eyes closed.
resting-baseline.description: The reference every other session is compared with: two minutes at rest, first with your eyes open on a cross, then closed until a tone tells you to open them.

0.text: Sit comfortably and let your shoulders drop.

1.text:
First, one minute with your eyes open on a cross.
Then one minute with your eyes closed.

2.text: Keep still and relax your face and jaw.

signal-navigator.title: Signal Navigator
signal-navigator.summary: A go/no-go attention game with paced breathing.
signal-navigator.description: Dock the cargo and let the debris pass. Paced breathing first, then two rounds of the game: it measures how well you hold a rule and withhold a response.
signal-navigator.contentWarning: Objects move across the screen for about five minutes. A reduced-motion mode is available, and you can stop at any time.

0.text: Cargo will cross your screen.

1.text:
Press Dock for blue cargo.
Let debris pass.

rule.label: The rule for the next route

0.text: Notice the urge to rush.

1.text:
For the next route:
Beacon first, cargo second.

0.text: Route complete.

config.footnote: This is not a medical test or diagnosis.

sustained-focus.title: Sustained Focus
sustained-focus.summary: Six unbroken minutes of go/no-go, with resting baselines and a mood check.
sustained-focus.description: Rest with your eyes closed, practise, then dock cargo for six minutes while rare debris asks you to hold back. Built to be measured: enough trials to see your brain's response to withholding and to a slip, and long enough to see focus drift.
sustained-focus.contentWarning: Objects move across the screen for about six minutes without a break. A reduced-motion mode is available, and you can stop at any time.

0.text: First you rest, then one long route.

config.prompt: Think of how you feel right now.

0.text: Cargo will cross your screen.

1.text:
Press Dock for blue cargo.
Let debris pass.

0.text:
That was practice.
The route ahead is about six minutes.

1.text:
Most of it is cargo.
Stay ready for the debris.

config.prompt: Think of how you feel now that the route is over.

0.text: Route complete.

config.footnote: This is not a medical test or diagnosis.

working-memory-span.title: Working Memory Span
working-memory-span.summary: Letters one at a time: is this the one from one step back? From two?
working-memory-span.description: The n-back. Easy first, then harder: you keep the last letters in mind and update them at every new one. Frontal theta rises with the load, which is exactly where a headband listens, and you rate how hard it felt at the end.

0.text: First you rest, then a memory game with letters, easy and then harder.
Letters appear one at a time.

1.text:
Press Match (or the space bar) when a letter
is the SAME AS THE ONE JUST BEFORE it.

2.text: Otherwise do nothing. A short practice first.

0.text:
Now press Match when a letter is the same
as the one TWO BEFORE it.

1.text:
B ... K ... B  is a match.
B ... B is not. It is meant to be hard.

config.prompt: Think of the last round, two back.

0.text: All done.

config.footnote: This is not a medical test or diagnosis.
